tone_statements.citation: Jambadu, J. B. 2024. Compounding in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Education, Winneba (data from Kpatoli, Pasaali and Gbieni dialects).
tone_statements.quote: Sɩsaalɩ is a tone language but owing to the limitation of time and space, this study couldn’t delve into effects of tone in Sɩsaalɩ compounding.

tone_statements.citation: Mustapha, N. 2018. The morpho-syntax of the noun phrase in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Ghana, Legon (Kpatolie south-western dialect).
tone_statements.quote: Sɩsaalɩ is a tonal language and tone plays important roles in the grammar and lexical inventory of the language. In Sɩsaalɩ, tone performs lexical functions which makes a distinction between words that are identical in nature. Also, tone performs a crucial role by marking grammatical categories such as tense and aspects, making a distinction between pronouns and imperatives. The grammatical tone as illustrated in examples 1 and 2 helps to make a distinction between the present and past tense of the verbs. [...] The present tense of the verbs is marked by a low tone, whereas past tense bear high tone on their final syllable.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.2.3 The Phonology of the Language, pp. 4-5

tone_statements.citation: Dumah, Iren B. 2017. Question markers in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Education, Winneba (data from the Paasaale dialect: Funsi, Kundugu, Yaala, Jumo, Buffiama).
tone_statements.quote: Although some languages construct polar questions by raising the pitch, that is, using rising intonation, the most consistent phonological strategy employed in coding polar interrogatives in Sɩsaalɩ is the high-low tone contour, accompanied by lengthening of the final sound. This pitch contour most often falls from a high to low on the final syllable of a phrase.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.1.1 Phonological strategy of forming polar questions in Sɩsaalɩ, p. 69

sources.citation: Jambadu, J. B. 2024. Compounding in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Education, Winneba (data from Kpatoli, Pasaali and Gbieni dialects).
sources.note: Discusses stress only as the English compound-stress criterion (Chomsky & Halle, Plag examples); never applies it to Sisaali. States 'Sisaali is a tone language' (p.124) and defers tonal effects to future work. Silent on Sisaali word stress.

tone.quote: Sɩsaalɩ is a tone language but owing to the limitation of time and space, this study couldn’t delve into effects of tone in Sɩsaalɩ compounding.
tone.says: Only a summary statement that Sisaali is a tone language, with tonal effects in compounding explicitly deferred to future work; mentions that after vowel elision 'the tone is maintained' and re-associates leftward. No inventory.

sources.citation: Mustapha, N. 2018. The morpho-syntax of the noun phrase in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Ghana, Legon (Kpatolie south-western dialect).
sources.note: Sec. 1.2.3 gives vowels, consonants, ATR harmony and 'Sisaali is a tonal language' with lexical and grammatical tone; no mention of stress or accent.

tone.quote: Sɩsaalɩ is a tonal language and tone plays important roles in the grammar and lexical inventory of the language. In Sɩsaalɩ, tone performs lexical functions which makes a distinction between words that are identical in nature. Also, tone performs a crucial role by marking grammatical categories such as tense and aspects, making a distinction between pronouns and imperatives. The grammatical tone as illustrated in examples 1 and 2 helps to make a distinction between the present and past tense of the verbs. [...] The present tense of the verbs is marked by a low tone, whereas past tense bear high tone on their final syllable.
tone.locator: sec. 1.2.3 The Phonology of the Language, pp. 4-5
tone.says: States that Sisaali is a tonal language with both lexical tone (distinguishing segmentally identical words) and grammatical tone (tense/aspect, pronoun vs imperative); present tense verbs carry low tone, past tense verbs a high tone on the final syllable; low tone usually left unmarked (citing Rowland 1966, Blass 1975, Moran 2006). No tone inventory count or tonal processes beyond H vs L.

sources.citation: Bushira, G. 2017. Some word formation processes in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Education, Winneba (Tumulung dialect = Sisaala Tumulung [sil], not paas1238).
sources.note: Silent on stress; says tone distinguishes lexical items and grammatical meaning, 'Sisaali can be said to be a tone language' (p.2); reports Luri 2011 on syllable structure incl. Paasaali.

sources.citation: Dumah, Iren B. 2017. Question markers in Sisaali. MPhil thesis, University of Education, Winneba (data from the Paasaale dialect: Funsi, Kundugu, Yaala, Jumo, Buffiama).
sources.note: Silent on word stress (the two 'stressed' mentions are general typology from Ultan/Siemund and echo questions). Only prosodic statement: polar questions are coded by a high-low tone contour with lengthening on the final syllable of the phrase.

tone.quote: Although some languages construct polar questions by raising the pitch, that is, using rising intonation, the most consistent phonological strategy employed in coding polar interrogatives in Sɩsaalɩ is the high-low tone contour, accompanied by lengthening of the final sound. This pitch contour most often falls from a high to low on the final syllable of a phrase.
tone.locator: sec. 4.1.1 Phonological strategy of forming polar questions in Sɩsaalɩ, p. 69
tone.says: First-hand Paasaal data, tone-marked; the prosodic finding is that polar questions are coded by a high-low (falling) tone contour with final lengthening on the last syllable of the phrase, declaratives ending in a low boundary tone and interrogatives in a low / high-low boundary tone; it presupposes lexical H/L tone but gives no tone inventory or tonology chapter.
tone.citation_as_reported: Dumah, Irene Basimaga. 2017. Question markers in Sɩsaalɩ. MPhil thesis, University of Education, Winneba (fieldwork in five Pasaale communities: Funsi, Kundugu, Yaala, Jumo, Buffiama).
